theme: A Halloween evening that welcomes everyone · Apply

cards.title: uncanny
cards.meaning: Strange and difficult to explain, often in a way that makes you feel uneasy.
cards.example: In the fog, the familiar path had an uncanny stillness, as if the whole forest were holding its breath.
cards.exercise: Choose the more natural use of uncanny and explain why: (a) The twins, who had never met, used exactly the same unusual expressions. (b) The bus arrived at its advertised time.
cards.answer: (a). Their unexpectedly exact similarity is difficult to explain. A bus arriving on schedule is ordinary, so uncanny would usually be inappropriate.
cards.conversation:
A: This is the path we walked yesterday, isn’t it?
B: Yes, but the fog makes it feel uncanny. I can barely see the next tree.
A: And there’s not a sound. Shall we head back?
B: Let’s. I’d rather take the road while it’s still light.
cards.notes: Use uncanny before a noun or after seem, feel or look. An uncanny resemblance is strikingly exact; it need not be frightening.
cards.wordForms: uncanny · more uncanny · most uncanny; noun: uncanniness
cards.synonymNote: Eerie emphasizes unease; uncanny can also describe a startling resemblance or ability.
cards.illustrationAlt: Mist makes the familiar forest difficult to recognize.

photoCredit.caption: Mist makes the familiar forest difficult to recognize.

cards.title: commemoration
cards.meaning: An act or event held to honor the memory of a person or a past event.
cards.example: The neighborhood held a candlelit commemoration for residents who had died during the previous year.
cards.exercise: An invitation reads: “Come to our commemoration—a loud costume contest with prizes!” What expectation does commemoration create, and which word better fits the advertised event?
cards.answer: Commemoration suggests honoring a person or past event. Celebration or party better fits the costume contest, unless remembrance is genuinely its purpose.
cards.conversation:
A: Are the candles part of the costume festival?
B: No. They’re for a separate commemoration in the square.
A: Is it appropriate for visitors to attend?
B: Yes. The organizers ask people to keep their voices low and leave the candles undisturbed.
cards.notes: Common patterns: a commemoration of an event; a ceremony in commemoration of someone. Do not assume Halloween and remembrance observances are the same tradition.
cards.synonymNote: A celebration may be joyful; a commemoration centers on remembering and honoring.
cards.illustrationAlt: Memorial candles express remembrance rather than a costume celebration.

photoCredit.caption: Memorial candles express remembrance rather than a costume celebration.

cards.title: factor in
cards.meaning: Include a relevant cost, condition or amount of time in a calculation or decision.
cards.example: When choosing our departure time, we factored in the walk to the venue and the queue at the entrance.
cards.exercise: The walk starts at 7:30. Getting there takes 15 minutes and entry takes another 10. What is the latest departure time? Explain your calculation in one sentence using factor in.
cards.answer: We should leave by 7:05 because we need to factor in both the fifteen-minute walk and the ten-minute queue.
cards.conversation:
A: The lantern walk starts at seven thirty. Leaving at seven twenty should be fine.
B: Have you factored in the fifteen-minute walk?
A: I hadn’t—and the organizers expect a ten-minute queue.
B: Then let’s work backward from the start time.
cards.notes: Separable: factor the delay in / factor in the delay. Put a pronoun in the middle: factor it in. Often used when planning or estimating.

factor in something

cards.title: iron out
cards.meaning: Resolve practical problems or disagreements so that an arrangement can work smoothly.
cards.example: The coordinators met to iron out an overlap in the volunteers’ shifts before opening night.
cards.exercise: Replace the vague reply “We’ll deal with it” with a specific two-sentence update using iron out. The problem: two volunteers have been assigned the same shift and the closing shift is empty.
cards.answer: We’ve ironed out the overlap by moving one volunteer to the closing shift. The early team will cover the first half hour until the replacement arrives.
cards.conversation:
A: Two volunteers are booked for the early shift, but nobody is staying until closing.
B: We need to iron that out before we send the rota.
A: I can move to the late shift if someone covers the first half hour.
B: I’ll cover it. That leaves us staffed throughout.
cards.notes: Separable: iron out the problems / iron the problems out; iron them out. Use it for resolving difficulties, not simply discovering them.

iron something out

cards.title: the devil is in the details
cards.meaning: A plan that appears straightforward may depend on small, easily overlooked details.
cards.example: The costume contest sounded open to everyone, but the devil was in the details: entrants needed to register before noon.
cards.exercise: Which overlooked detail best justifies this idiom? A: The poster is orange. B: Registration closes six hours before the contest. C: The event has a cheerful name. Give one practical consequence.
cards.answer: B. Someone arriving at the contest without registering earlier could be unable to enter, even though admission is free.
cards.conversation:
A: Entry is free, so we can register when we get there.
B: Read the small print. Registration closes at noon.
A: Ah, the devil is in the details. I only noticed “free entry.”
B: We still have twenty minutes. Let’s register now.
cards.notes: Often used as a warning after broad agreement with a proposal. It draws attention to implementation; it does not mean every plan is doomed.
synonyms: small points can cause big problems
cards.illustrationAlt: Small print can contain a condition that changes the whole plan.

cards.title: a double-edged sword
cards.meaning: Something that brings an advantage while also creating a related disadvantage or risk.
cards.example: Posting the party photos online is a double-edged sword: it spreads the word, but guests may lose control of where their images appear.
cards.exercise: Complete this balanced assessment with one benefit and one drawback: “A public event hashtag is a double-edged sword: ___, yet ___.” Keep both points connected to public visibility.
cards.answer: A public event hashtag is a double-edged sword: it helps people discover the event, yet it can expose participants’ photos to strangers.
cards.conversation:
A: Last year’s photos brought in twice as many visitors. We should post everything again.
B: Publicity is a double-edged sword. Some guests don’t want their children’s faces online.
A: Could we use close-ups of the decorations instead?
B: Yes, and ask permission before including anyone identifiable.
cards.notes: Name both edges: a benefit and a cost of the same thing. Two unrelated complaints do not demonstrate the idiom.
cards.illustrationAlt: Online sharing offers visibility but can reduce control over an image.

photoCredit.description: Young man checking smartphone at modern desk setup, focusing on work.Stock Photo
photoCredit.caption: Online sharing offers visibility but can reduce control over an image.

cards.title: I see your point, although I would qualify it slightly.
cards.meaning: A polite way to accept the main part of an argument while limiting or refining one of its claims.
cards.example: “I see your point, although I would qualify it slightly. Bright lighting helps people find the entrance, but flashing lights are not necessary.”
cards.exercise: A colleague claims, “Every part of the event must be scary.” Respond with the target phrase, preserve the useful part of the idea, and add one clear limitation.
cards.answer: I see your point, although I would qualify it slightly. A spooky atmosphere suits the main attraction, but a quiet area would let guests step away when they need to.
cards.conversation:
A: A good Halloween event needs to be frightening from beginning to end.
B: I see your point, although I would qualify it slightly. A family event also needs a quiet place to take a break.
A: Wouldn’t that spoil the atmosphere?
B: Not if it’s separate from the main attraction. Guests could choose how much intensity they want.
cards.notes: Qualify means limit or make more precise here. Follow the phrase with an actual qualification; without one, it can sound evasive or overly formal.
synonyms: I broadly agree, but with a reservation.
That is persuasive, subject to one qualification.
cards.illustrationAlt: A discussion leaves room to agree while adding a reservation.

photoCredit.description: Two diverse colleagues engaging in a thoughtful discussion in a modern office setting.Stock Photo
photoCredit.caption: A discussion leaves room to agree while adding a reservation.

cards.title:
Double, double toil and trouble;
Fire burn, and cauldron bubble.
cards.meaning: A rhythmic chant that creates a supernatural atmosphere in a scene from Macbeth.
cards.example: During rehearsal, the actors stressed “Double, double” and the repeated b sounds to give the witches’ chant its driving rhythm.
cards.exercise: You are directing this line for a school performance. Identify one repetition and one repeated consonant sound. Explain how you would use them in delivery.
cards.answer: Repeat and stress “Double, double” to establish a pulse. Emphasize the b sound in “burn” and “bubble” to make the chant feel insistent and spell-like.
cards.conversation:
A: Shall I whisper the whole line to make it sound sinister?
B: Try stressing “Double, double” first. The repetition gives it a pulse.
A: And make “burn” and “bubble” sharper?
B: Exactly. Let the sounds create the tension rather than simply making your voice louder.
cards.notes: Macbeth, Act 4, Scene 1; first published in the First Folio (1623). The speakers are the witches, not Shakespeare speaking personally. Toil means hard work; a cauldron is a large pot.
cards.synonymNote: These describe the kind of speech; they are not substitute quotations.
cards.attribution: William Shakespeare · Macbeth, Act IV, Scene 1 (First Folio) · Published 1623
cards.illustrationAlt: A cauldron is a large cooking pot: the central object in the witches’ chant.

photoCredit.caption: A cauldron is a large cooking pot: the central object in the witches’ chant.

cards.title: Inversion after only then
cards.meaning: When Only then opens a clause meaning “not until that moment,” place the auxiliary before the subject.
cards.example: I tried walking in the full costume. Only then did I realize that the mask blocked my view.
cards.exercise: Rewrite as one sentence beginning Only then: “We tested the costume in the dark. At that moment, we noticed that the sleeves covered the reflective strips.”
cards.answer: Only then did we notice that the sleeves covered the reflective strips. Use notice, not noticed, after did.
cards.conversation:
A: Did the costume work when you tried it on?
B: It looked fine in the mirror. Then I tried going down the steps.
A: What happened?
B: Only then did I realize I couldn’t see my feet through the mask.
cards.notes: Past simple: Only then did + subject + base verb. Past perfect: Only then had + subject + past participle. No inversion in “I only then realized…”; this fronted pattern is more emphatic.
cards.illustrationAlt: Trying a costume on is only the first step; it must also work in motion.

photoCredit.caption: Trying a costume on is only the first step; it must also work in motion.

cards.title: What would you like to do for Halloween?
cards.meaning: An open invitation to share Halloween preferences without assuming that the other person celebrates it.
cards.example: “What would you like to do for Halloween—if you’re doing anything this year?”
cards.exercise: Your neighbor replies, “I don’t celebrate Halloween, actually.” Write a friendly response that acknowledges this and smoothly opens a different topic.
cards.answer: Of course. Are you doing anything nice this weekend instead?
cards.conversation:
A: What would you like to do for Halloween, if you’re doing anything this year?
B: Something low-key. I’m not really into haunted houses.
A: Same here. How about carving a pumpkin and making dinner?
B: That sounds more like me. Have you ever managed one of those elaborate designs?
A: Once. It looked impressive for about ten minutes before it collapsed.
B: Then let’s start with a face we can actually finish.
cards.notes: Offer a low-pressure follow-up. If someone says they do not celebrate, accept the answer and move to another topic rather than asking them to justify it.
cards.illustrationAlt: Pumpkin carving offers a quieter alternative to a haunted attraction.

photoCredit.caption: Pumpkin carving offers a quieter alternative to a haunted attraction.

cards.title: A little room to choose
cards.meaning: A four-paragraph model with a main idea, two developed points, and a conclusion.
cards.example: We use “A Halloween evening that welcomes everyone” when we discuss this idea.
cards.exercise: Outline four paragraphs improving a school fair. Include two different changes, a concrete example for each, and a conclusion linking their benefits.
cards.answer: Introduction: a more welcoming fair. Body 1: clear signs at the entrance. Body 2: quiet seating away from the stage. Conclusion: better guidance and choice help guests enjoy themselves.
cards.notes: Each body paragraph needs a distinct supporting point and a concrete example. The conclusion draws the argument together without introducing a third proposal.
cards.structure: State a position; develop two distinct points with concrete examples; draw them together in the conclusion.
paragraphs: A welcoming Halloween event gives people choices rather than testing everyone’s courage. At our neighborhood gathering, we wanted a lively atmosphere without pressuring guests to enjoy the same activities. Clear options and careful preparation proved more useful than an increasingly elaborate spectacle.

First, we made two experiences easy to identify. A lantern-lit route led to the main attraction; a quieter room offered pumpkin carving and warm drinks. Volunteers explained both at the entrance, allowing guests to change their minds without having to justify their preferences.

Practical details mattered just as much. Only when we tested a costume outside did we notice that its mask restricted the wearer’s view. We adjusted it and checked the route for obstacles. Ingredient labels and non-food treats also helped guests decide what suited them.

The event worked because its atmosphere invited participation while its arrangements preserved a sense of control. Preparation did not remove the surprise; it removed avoidable pressure. Next year, we would retain that balance: make the possibilities clear, anticipate small obstacles, and leave people room to choose.
cards.illustrationAlt: A distinctive costume can be part of an evening with room for different preferences.

photoCredit.caption: A distinctive costume can be part of an evening with room for different preferences.
